question: What evidence separates a prototype, transfer to another builder and reliable service?
useful_similarities: Both concern precision instruments transferred from successful makers to other users/builders, with observable operation and opportunities for subsequent failure.
important_differences: K1 was a commissioned close copy tested over long voyages; TEA designs varied across laboratories and enabled several downstream research tasks. Eighteenth-century navigation and 1970s laboratory resources, markets and standards differ.
evidence_comparability: Object/obituary and scholarly voyage synthesis versus contemporary interviews and partial follow-up; neither supplies matched cost/lifetime trials.
connections_nonindependence: Separate source families, but both selected to reveal difficult reproduction. Collins 1974 and 1975 are not independent studies; K1 sources may share Board reports.
omitted_countercases: Routine successful replication from complete documentation; cheap instruments bought without workshop training; failed makers who left no record.
conclusion_limit: Both separate technical principle from production/use, but do not establish that tacit transfer is always necessary or quantify an effect of contact.

question: Does more elaborate precision make a design more practically adoptable?
useful_similarities: Specific design attributes mattered only in relation to the task and reproducible operation; alternative designs and manual practices remained available.
important_differences: Tanaka automated a recurring adjustment under seasonal conventions; K1 carried reference time at sea; TEA tolerances concerned uncertain electrode requirements. Their accuracy and reliability measures are not interchangeable.
evidence_comparability: Artifact mechanisms and a biographical single-product outcome, named voyages and qualitative laboratory contrasts; no common precision/price metric.
connections_nonindependence: Japanese clock sources overlap museum materials; Higgitt's synthesis combines earlier chronometer narratives. No known direct transmission from these early clocks to the observed TEA episodes is claimed.
omitted_countercases: Widely sold automatic seasonal clocks, inaccessible buyers' records, and laboratory settings where tight dimensional tolerances demonstrably are necessary.
conclusion_limit: The cases reject a universal monotonic equation of greater complexity/precision with greater uptake; they do not show that precision usually reduces adoption.

question: How do interchangeable production and workshop adaptation distribute the work of making parts fit?
useful_similarities: Both address fit, component variation, tools and inspection/reputation; practical operation requires work beyond possession of a mechanical principle.
important_differences: Armory production sought repeatable specifications under a state purchaser, whereas Tanzanian repair dealt with mixed aged products and changing spare-part markets. Production flow and repair flow solve different tasks.
evidence_comparability: Armory documentary synthesis and surviving gauges versus retrospective histories and workshop observation; neither provides matched lifetime cost or injury data.
connections_nonindependence: US sources repeatedly draw on Smith; Tanzanian claims draw mainly on one Grace research programme. Shared interpretive terms are not independent proof.
omitted_countercases: Well-supplied garages using inexpensive new standard parts; independent repair of highly standardised equipment; factories where workers retain substantial fitting discretion.
conclusion_limit: Standardisation can relocate fitting effort to tooling/inspection, while repair can retain or recreate adaptation work. Neither configuration warrants a general skill or welfare ranking.

question: When does repair extend access, and when does it conceal a continuing service or livelihood burden?
useful_similarities: Tanzanian repair economies combine purchased artifacts, practical learning, tools/parts and cash-constrained users; restored function is observed or reported.
important_differences: Motor vehicles carry heavy mechanical loads and passengers; appliances depend on electric supply and use different training/diagnostic systems. Grace's earlier histories and 2011–2012 observations differ from Mchome's2018/2020 interviews.
evidence_comparability: Independent appliance interviews provide some new evidence, but not an equivalent sample or measured repair survival; no common adoption or income denominator.
connections_nonindependence: Mchome cites Grace for automotive and informal-training history. Only Mchome's original appliance interviews are a distinct evidence stream; the same city's economy also connects cases materially.
omitted_countercases: Failed repairs, people unable to pay even small repair charges, women running workshops, full cohorts of displaced utility workers and devices discarded because repair costs exceed replacement.
conclusion_limit: Repair can preserve a real service without fixing upstream infrastructure or guaranteeing good work. Growing repair employment is not by itself evidence of improved welfare or smooth occupational adjustment.
